tasks.title: Mars motion as seen from the Earth
tasks.statement: Assuming that the orbits of Earth and Mars are circular, picture 12.a shows such orbits to scale; positions of the Sun and of the Earth and Mars when Mars is at opposition are also represented. In table 12.b you will report distance from Earth and angular data for Mars: Column 1: day of observation (in the interval +105 days from time of opposition t0). Column 2: distance to Mars from Earth, to be given in km. Column 3: position angle a of Mars, to be given in degrees. Column 4: day/days in which Mars is in quadrature with the Sun as seen from Earth (to be indicated by the symbol Q) or it appears “stationing” (to be indicated by the symbol S). In picture 12.c report the distance (in au, Y axis) Mars-Earth D as a function of the position angle a (in degrees, X axis).

parts.question: Taking into account the sidereal periods of the Earth and Mars with a good approximation and starting from the initial configuration where Mars is in opposition (i.e. along the up-down direction the orbit representation), compute the positions of the two planets every 15 days for a time interval of +105 days and draw them on picture 12.a.
parts.reference: The sidereal period of Mars, with a good approximation, can be obtained from the III Kepler law considering that orbits of Earth and Mars are in scale. Starting from the configuration where Mars is in opposition, the positions of the two planets every 15 days are as follows. Criteria: Positioning of Earth and Mars on the graph (up to 4 points).

parts.question: In picture 12.a draw the lines connecting the positions of Earth and Mars at the same epoch and, for each epoch, measure the Earth-Mars distance D and report it, in km, in column 2 of table 12.b.
parts.reference: By measuring in the graph the Earth-Mars distance D, it then can be converted to km considering that the Sun-Earth distance is equal to 1 AU. Criteria: Values of the distance (up to 2 points).

parts.question: Measure the position angle a of Mars as seen from the Earth with reference to the up-down direction and report it, in degrees, in column 3 of table 12.b.
parts.reference: Once the position of the two planets every 15 days are known, the angle alpha of Mars as seen from the Earth with reference to the up-down direction can be measured. Criteria: Values of the alpha angle (up to 2 points).

parts.question: For which of the positions of Earth and Mars at the same epoch you have drawn Mars would be in quadrature with the Sun and mark them with the symbol Q in column 4 of table 12.b.
parts.reference: Looking at the positions of Earth and Mars at the same epoch, Mars would be in quadrature (or nearby) for t0 - 105d and for t0 + 105d. Criteria: Identification of the days of quadrature (up to 1 point).

parts.question: Infer the days when Mars appears stationing in the sky during the considered time interval (+105 days) and mark them with the symbol S in column 4 of table 12.b.
parts.reference: Once the distance Mars-Earth as a function of the position angle is plotted in Figure 12.c, the days, with the precision allowed by the data, when Mars appears stationing in the sky are inferred. Criteria: Identification of the days of stationing (up to 1 point).

parts.question: Plot position angle of Mars as function of Earth-Mars distance in picture 12.c, and provide an estimation of the duration of the apparent retrograde motion of Mars T(retrograde) and write it, in days, in the box at the bottom of picture 12.c.
parts.reference: The motion in the sky of Mars appears retrograde among the points of stationing. T (retrograde) = 75 days. Criteria: Plot of position angle of Mars as function of Earth-Mars distance (1 point); Time interval of retrograde motion of Mars (1 point, the point will be given only if the reported value, 75 days +/- 15, is inferred from correct assumptions).

tasks.title: Observations at the INAF — Abruzzo Astronomical Observatory (OAAB)
tasks.statement: The observation nights of December 23, 2021, January 24, 2022 and November 25, 2022 are made available at the "TNT" telescope of the OAAb (geographical coordinates: lambda = 13 degrees 44', phi = 42 degrees 39'). The TNT has a Ritchey-Chretien optical design, with a primary diameter of 720 mm and a secondary of 185 mm. The overall focal length is 9800 mm. At the focal plane is mounted a back-illuminated E2V CCD47 with 2048x2048 square pixels of 20x20 micron size each. You are the scientific manager of a project that aims to study the optical bands of open stellar clusters of our galaxy listed in Table 13.a. Write in Table 13.b the answers to the questions.

parts.question: Choose for each of the three available dates listed in column 1 the globular cluster that at 00:00 Local Time is the nearest at culmination and write its name in column 2 of Table 13.b.
parts.reference: On Dec 23 the mean Sun has a RA of about 18h. Hence at local midnight the stars closest to culmination have RA ~ 6h... Criteria: Identification of the first cluster (2 points), Identification of the second cluster (2 points), Identification of the third cluster (2 points).

parts.question: For each of the three selected clusters infer if it can fit entirely into the field of view of the CCD and write the answer as YES or NOT in column 3 of Table 13.b.
parts.reference: The length of each CCD side is 2048 * 20 * 10^-6 m ~ 41 mm. Taking into account the focal length of the telescope the FoV is a square with a side of alpha = arctan(41 mm / 9800 mm) ~ 14'. Criteria: Indication if the first cluster can be observed with a single acquisition (1 point), Indication if the second cluster can be observed with a single acquisition (1 point), Indication if the third cluster can be observed with a single acquisition (1 point).

parts.question: Calculate the radius in light years of the three selected clusters and write them in column 4 of Table 13.b.
parts.reference: Given the angular diameter beta and the distance D of the clusters, the radius R, after transforming the distance in ly can be computed using the formula: R = D * tan(beta / 2). Criteria: Estimation of first cluster radius in light years (1 point, 0.5 points max if the value is not provided in light years), Estimation of second cluster radius in light years (1 point, 0.5 points max if the value is not provided in light years), Estimation of third cluster radius in light years (1 point, 0.5 points max if the value is not provided in light years).

tasks.title: Galilean Moons
tasks.statement: Let's assume Jupiter equator and the orbits of its four Galilean Moons be coincident with the ecliptic. The position of Galilean Moons on 1st of November 2021, as observed from Earth, is shown in Figure 14.1. The in-scale corresponding orbital configuration, as could be observed from a distant point located on the extension Jupiter rotation axis, is shown in Figure 14.2, where the direction to Earth is represented as a dot-and-dash line. The basic data for the four Galilean Moons of Jupiter are given in Table 14.a. All moons orbits have a very low eccentricity and then they can be considered circular. The Jupiter average radius is assumed to be 69173 km.

parts.question: Draw in Figure 14.3 what will be the observed orbital configurations for observations made at the same hour on the following dates: 3rd of November 2021, 4th of November 2021, 5th of November 2021, 8th of November 2021, 9th of November 2021, 10th of November 2021, 12th of November 2021.
parts.reference: Starting from the sidereal periods listed in Table 14.a, the angular velocity of each satellite around Jupiter can be computed. Then, from the initial configuration shown in Figure 14.1 and 14.2, all the other configurations can be inferred. Criteria: Positioning of Galilean moons on 3 nov graph (1.5 points), 4 nov graph (1.5 points), 5 nov graph (1.5 points), 8 nov graph (1.5 points), 9 nov graph (1.5 points), 10 nov graph (1.5 points), 12 nov graph (1.5 points).

parts.question: Which one of the 2021 configurations is similar to one of the 1610 configurations? Write in English the two dates in the box below Figure 14.4.
parts.reference: Among the computed 2021 configurations, the one of 9 nov appears quite similar (although not identical) to the second configuration observed by Galileo on 15 Jan 1610. Criteria: Identification of 1610 configuration corresponding to the 9 nov 2021 one (up to 1.5 points - note: total weight in table is 1.5 points).
